extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, state environmental and public utility regulators, FERC, regional transmission operators, and electric utilities (NRECA members)
extracted.subtask_short: comment on EPA Clean Power Plan 111(d)
extracted.subtask_description: Public-comment letter giving legal, practical, and policy criteria that EPA and States must satisfy in drafting and implementing 111(d) emission guidelines (the Clean Power Plan). Focuses on statutory authority, timelines, feasibility, reliability, NSR interactions, SIP/FIP content, and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: State legislative authority and interagency coordination required
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation of the Proposal will require new legislation to authorize involved state agencies, both air pollution and public utility regulators, to devise and implement the types of measures in the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must enact statutory authority to incorporate the Proposal’s building blocks into SIPs; multi-state systems and entities operating in more than one State increase complexity exponentially. EPA should recognize this requirement and not assume existing authorities suffice. Examples: inclusion of independent power producers, renewable project developers, and non-utility electricity suppliers requires legislative means to bring them into a state 111(d) SIP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate time for state plan development (recommended deadlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposal’s one-year plan-development period following issuance of final rules is woefully inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA recommends at least five years for individual States to develop implementation plans and seven years for States choosing multi-State plans. EPA should adjust State final compliance goals accordingly to reflect longer plan-development timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for extensions when States cannot meet final goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule makes no provision for States that are unable, despite best efforts, to meet final emission reduction goals by the final compliance year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final emission guidelines should provide procedures for States that demonstrate they have made good faith efforts but not achieved targets to request and obtain extensions of time. NRECA suggests EPA should grant extensions of up to five years for States that demonstrate good-faith implementation and are on a glidepath to compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon interim goals and allow States to set standards of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s interim goals (e.g., 2020 interim targets and interim BSER goals) are legally and practically problematic and should be abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should (1) revise the Proposed Rule to allow States to set the standards of performance and determine timing/source-by-source application, and (2) eliminate interim goals altogether. Interim goals impose rushed requirements, force two-thirds of reductions early (within two–three years after plan approval), and negate meaningful state-devised alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must document and justify any phase‑in schedules or infrastructure assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s proposed phase-in schedule for Building Block 2 (based on infrastructure improvements) lacks documentation and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States cannot determine needed infrastructure or build timelines on the record provided. EPA must supply documentation for any phase-in schedules, explain assumptions about infrastructure, and provide evidence for claimed timelines before imposing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of book life vs. remaining useful life in glidepaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility 'book life' (an accounting depreciation metric) is an inadequate proxy for remaining useful life and should not be used alone to set compliance glidepaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must account for remaining useful life, investment recovery dynamics (market vs. tariffed recovery), and reliability needs. Basing glidepaths on book life can leave owners unable to recover investments and fail to account for continued operation beyond book life; EPA should instead provide guidance on how to consider remaining useful life and other factors permitted by the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify NSR interactions and exempt HRI projects as routine maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat-rate improvement (HRI) projects and other efficiency upgrades undertaken to comply with the emission guidelines risk triggering New Source Review (NSR), creating litigation risk and economic disincentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must clarify that HRI projects undertaken for compliance are exempt from NSR as routine maintenance OR require that NSR compliance costs be included when determining feasibility and cost-effectiveness. NRECA documents EPA’s prior NSR enforcement history (400+ targeted projects since 1999 and additional alleged projects) and warns that overlapping NSR liability will produce stranded assets and premature closures if not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA should publish a model SIP and specify likely FIP elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule contains no model state plan or outline of what EPA would lawfully prescribe as a Federal Implementation Plan (FIP) if a State fails to submit an acceptable SIP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should issue a supplemental proposal specifying the common elements of a federal plan it would prescribe—identify which Building Blocks would be included, legal rationale, how it would calculate a State’s emission-reduction goal under a FIP, and how it would consider remaining useful life and other Section 111 factors—so States know the minimum elements required for approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER must be achievable considering cost and energy impacts (takings risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards and emission guidelines must be based on a BSER that is 'achievable' given cost and energy-usage considerations; overly burdensome standards may constitute a compensable regulatory taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must assess economic impacts on property owners, interference with investment-backed expectations, and the character of government action (the three Lingle takings factors). The Proposed Rule should avoid forcing retirements or imposing requirements that make units commercially infeasible to operate, or it risks takings liability and compensation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for transmission lead times and state siting/regulatory hurdles
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding renewable, nuclear, or other non‑GHG-emitting generation requires additional transmission capacity, which is generally authorized and regulated by state public utility commissions and subject to lengthy siting/permitting processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA and States must account for typical transmission timelines (average 5–7 years; often 6–8.5+ years where federal lands are involved) and the frequent local opposition to new lines. Without planning for realistic transmission build-out timelines, additional generation cannot deliver emissions reductions and States cannot rely on Building Block 3 being realizable within short compliance windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of non-utility electricity providers into SIPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many entities implicated by Building Blocks 2–4 (independent power producers, renewable developers, non-utility electricity suppliers) are not currently subject to state public utility regulation and thus must be brought into state plans deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States will need new legislative authority and regulatory structures to include these diverse entities in SIPs and coordinate their activities. EPA should acknowledge this need and provide guidance on mechanisms to integrate non-utility providers into state 111(d) implementation plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand‑side energy efficiency requires integrated, ongoing programs and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieving Building Block 4’s 1.5% annual electricity usage reduction requires integrated demand-side programs that include all electricity providers and continue year-to-year, not a one-time measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must develop structures to include all types of electricity providers in efficiency programs and secure legislative authority to do so. EPA should recognize that such programs are ongoing obligations (not one-time) and allow appropriate time and legal mechanisms for states to implement them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a dynamic reliability safety valve and allow staged implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must include a reliability safety valve (RSV) to avoid undermining bulk electric system reliability and to give States flexibility to respond to regional reliability concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety valve options include: (a) an RSV modeled on MATS that allows short additional implementation time without enforcement risk; (b) requiring FERC certification that SIPs (individually and collectively) will not harm reliability before plans take effect; (c) ISO/RTO/operator-led reliability assessments integrated into plan approval; and (d) an associated cost safety valve. States should be permitted to stage implementation past 2030 as necessary to protect reliability and account for remaining useful lives of EGUs.
